demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
The Weight of the Scissors

Mei is nineteen years old and works at a small salon in the strip mall near her family's apartment. She has been cutting and styling hair since she was sixteen, first watching her aunt, then practicing on cousins and neighbors, and finally earning her license the month before everything changed. She was good at it — precise, careful, someone who took pride in the steadiness of her hands.

Eight months ago, on an otherwise ordinary Tuesday afternoon, a client shifted unexpectedly in the chair at exactly the wrong moment. Mei was trimming close to the ear with shears when the woman turned, and the blade caught the side of her face. The cut was deep — deep enough that there was a great deal of blood, deep enough that the woman needed emergency surgery, deep enough that the word "disfigurement" appeared in the paperwork that followed. Mei had done everything right. The salon owner said so. The licensing board agreed. It was an accident, fully documented as such. None of that has mattered to Mei in the months since.

She still remembers the sound — a sound she cannot quite describe but cannot stop hearing — and the way the blood appeared so suddenly, so much of it, spreading across the white salon cape. She froze for several seconds before she screamed for help. Those seconds haunt her. She replays them constantly, inserting different choices, different outcomes, as though her mind believes it can still go back and fix it.

Mei returned to work after two weeks because she needed the income and because her mother told her that staying home would only make things worse. Her mother was trying to help. But standing behind the chair now, Mei's hands tremble before every cut. She finds herself holding her breath when she lifts the shears, and some days she has to set them down and excuse herself to the back room, where she sits on an overturned bucket and waits for her heart to stop pounding. Her coworkers have noticed. She can tell by the way they speak carefully around her.

At night, she sleeps poorly and briefly. She wakes from dreams in which the accident replays itself, sometimes exactly as it happened, sometimes with worse outcomes — the woman blinded, or Mei unable to stop cutting, her hands moving without her permission. She wakes with her heart slamming and lies still in the dark beside her boyfriend, Darius, who has learned not to touch her suddenly when she is like this. He is patient with her, more patient than she feels she deserves. She has told him she doesn't understand why he stays. He tells her she is still the same person. She does not believe him.

Mei has largely stopped seeing friends outside of work. She canceled plans so many times that the invitations stopped coming, which she tells herself is a relief and which she knows is not. She scrolls through her phone in the evenings without absorbing anything, sitting close to Darius but feeling separated from him by something she cannot name. Food tastes like very little. She has lost weight her small frame could not spare.

What troubles her most, she says, is not the nightmares or even the trembling hands — it is the belief that has settled into her like sediment: that she is someone who hurts people. That her steadiness was always an illusion. She thinks about the woman's face every day, wonders whether the scar is still visible, whether the woman hates her. She has not allowed herself to find out. She is afraid of what she might learn, and equally afraid of what it would mean if she stopped being afraid to ask.

She still goes to work. She still picks up the shears. That, she says, is the only thing she feels certain about anymore — that she keeps showing up, even when every part of her is braced for something terrible to happen again.
